replying_to: Replying to FLBoost: On-the-Fly Fine-tuning Boosts Federated Learning via Data-free Distillation
display_title: Official Review of Paper491 by Reviewer QdK9

content.summary_of_the_paper: To tackle the heterogeneity challenge, this paper proposes on-the-fly fine-tuning the global model in server via data-free distillation to boost performance. Specifically, it utilizes an adversarial distillation scheme to generate pseudo data to fine-tune the global model. To maintain the consistency between the generated data and the overall data distribution of the clients, it utilizes focused knowledge distillation which considers the proportion of the amount of data in each category. In addition, it performs an attention-based ensemble according to the number of samples in each category of each client. This paper tries to solve data heterogeneity from the perspective of the server and it can achieve acceptable performance.
content.main_review:
The work is interesting and makes sense to some extent. However, it still suffers from the following limitations: 
1. The method is not novelty enough. Data generalization in an adversarial style is a common way to obtain data and it has been introduced to federated learning. To obtain better performance, this paper only takes the proportion of data in each category into consideration, which may be not novelty enough.
2. It is better to explain whether the data heterogeneity means label distribution shifts, the imbalance of the category, or other offsets. Data heterogeneity is a wide concept while this paper mainly focuses on label distribution shifts among clients.
3. Please explain the meaning of 'wrong' in 'FedGen ignores the wrong knowledge in data heterogeneity scenario'. What is "wrong"?
4. Please explain the meaning of R in Equation (4). This symbol is introduced and used without any explanation.
5. Since there exists much work about label distribution shifts, it is better to utilize some common datasets and settings with existing work. For example, FedGen utilizes MNIST and some other datasets while MOON utilizes CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-Imagenet. There is no need to perform all experiments from scratch, which may make results unconvincing.
6. Please explain how to evaluate the performance. According to Equation (1), the goal of federated learning is to perform well on all clients, which means there needs a special test dataset for each client. In this situation, some methods, such as FedBN, which obtain different models for different clients may obtain better results.
7. Since the paper focuses on label distribution shifts, it is better to evaluate on more datasets, including imbalance datasets. In addition, it is better that test sets and training sets have different label distributions. In reality, we have no prior on real data distribution in the server and it might be wrong to treat the combined data of all clients as the real distribution.
8. Since the method generates data in the server with a large amount of computation, it is better to show time complexity of the proposed method.
9. Some explanations of results are not clear enough. For example, FedGen is better than FedGen* while FLBoost-f is worse than FLBoost. In addition, it is better to add SCAFFOLD+FedGen* in Table 3.
10. There are still some other problems to solve. For example, it is better to show the entire training process in Figure 3. In Table 4, it is better to keep the same setting with other experiments.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I recommend rejecting the current version of the paper based on the above analysis.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 3 - Part Two
content.comment:
6. The goal of this paper is to perform well on data of all clients using one model, which is the goal of federated learning (FL). FedBN is a personal federated learning (PFL) method, where many models of different architectures can be built. FL and PFL are different tasks and can be applied in different scenarios.

7. Thank you for this constructive comment. Due to time limit, we may be unable to test FLBoost in such real-world scenarios. However, performance in these scenarios is an important evaluation metric, and we will put it into our future work.

8. The extra time cost of FLBoost is $I\*(I_g\*t_g+I_d\*t_d)$, where $t_g$ and $t_d$ are the training time of generator and global model respectively. In our experiment settings, the training time in one communication round for FedAVG, FedProx, FedDyn, SCAFFOLD, FedGen, FedDF and FLBoost are  are 78, 82, 83, 93, 165, 188, 194 seconds respectively. The last three DFKD based methods require roughly double time of the first four methods. The experiments are conducted on a machine with Intel(R) Xeon(R) CPU E5-2690 0 $@$ 2.90GHz, 32GB main memory and GPU GTX TITAN.

9. Currently, it is unclear why FLBoost and FedGen show different trends for feature-level generation. One possible reason is the difference when handling wrong knowledge. FLBoost facilitates maximization of knowledge and filters wrong knowledge in local models. As a result, the pseudo data is effective to train global model. The pseudo image can train all layers of global model, while the pseudo feature can only train the last few layers. Thus FLBoost achieves higher performance than FLBoost-f. On the contrary, the pseudo data may fail to capture the real data distribution, and the pseudo image will hurt the local model more than the pseudo feature. Thus FedGen* yields lower performance than FedGen. We add the results of SCAFFOLD+FedGen* in the revision.

10. The entire training process of Figure 3 is added in Appendix A.9. In this figure, FLBoost exceeds the other methods in about 150 and 100 rounds for CIFAR10 and CIFAR100, and it achieves distinct performance gain after 1000 rounds. Please see Appendix A.9 for detailed results. Due to the time limit, we may be unable to change Table 4 in the revision, and we will put it into our future work.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 3 - Part One
content.comment:
Thank you for your effort put into this paper and the constructive comments to this work. The comments about paper writing, organization and experiment are especially valuable for us. The following are detailed response to each comment.

1. The proposed method FLBoost fine-tune the global model in server via data-free knowledge distillation. The data generation is in an adversarial manner, and the generation and distillation are reweighted according to the data distribution. In the future we will put more effort to extend this work.

2. In this paper, we follow SCAFFOLD and FedGen that use "Data Heterogeneity'' to represent the scenario where the data in clients are not identically and independently distributed (non-iid). Considering the label distribution shift in data heterogeneity, we propose FocusedKD and EnsembleAtt for more effective distillation. However, FLBoost is proposed to deal with the board scenario of non-iid FL. Because it generates pseudo data to capture the data distribution of clients, and uses them to train the global model, it can mitigate the impact of data distribution discrepancy.

3. In FLBoost and FedGen, the generator is trained using the local models of clients active in current round. FedGen uses the statistics of *whole data on all clients* to compute the sampling probability $p(y)$, while FLBoost customizes the sampling probability $p_t(y)$ according to the training data in round $t$. However, data in client may be class-imbalanced in data heterogeneity scenario. As a result, the active clients in one round may have limited even no data for some classes. For these minority classes, the knowledge in client models is wrong and misleading, especially in the first few rounds. In FedGen, the wrong knowledge will be used to generate data and train the local model, which will damage the original local training in contrast.

4. $R$ is an image regularization term to improve the quality of pseudo data, such as fidelity, diversity, etc. For example, DeepDream[1] use image prior to steer pseudo data away from unrealistic images. In this paper, we use the diversity loss in FedGen to improve the diversity of generated data. It restricts that the distance between two pseudo data $\widetilde{x}_i$ and $\widetilde{x}_j$ should be the same with the distance for noise $z_i$ and $z_j$, where $\widetilde{x}_i$ is generated using $z_i$.

5. Experiments in this paper follow the setting in FedDyn, including dataset, dataset assignment and hyperparameter. Considering the effect of random varieties (random seed, network initialization, etc.), we rerun baselines for fair comparison, using the same random varieties and random the varieties three times. The code of FLBoost can be released upon acceptance, as stated on page 10. In the future, we will put effort to extend the experiments on settings of more methods.

[1] https://ai.googleblog.com/2015/06/inceptionism-going-deeper-into-neural.html

replying_to: Replying to FLBoost: On-the-Fly Fine-tuning Boosts Federated Learning via Data-free Distillation
display_title: Official Review of Paper491 by Reviewer Aw8p

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper tackles the data heterogeneity challenge in federated learning from the aspect of model aggregation on the central server, which is different from many existing works focusing on the model update on the client. The authors propose a data-free knowledge distillation method dubbed FLBoost to enhance the model aggregation step. Specifically, a generator with an adaptive sampling scheme is trained to recover diverse yet fidelity data in the image space, and an attention-based ensemble scheme is leveraged for model aggregation. FLBoost is orthogonal to many client-level methods. Experiments on CIFAR datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of FLBoost.
content.main_review:
## Strengths
* Writing is well-organized and easy to follow.
* FLBoost is effective on CIFAR datasets and outperforms other server-level methods under the same condition. Also, FLBoost is compatible with client-level methods, which is a benefit.

## Weaknesses
* This paper has marginal novelty. The proposed method FLBoost is incremental compared with FedGen [1] which also uses the data-free distillation. FLBoost uses the reweighting schemes for image generation or model aggregation, which are common operations and not novel. The remaining novelty seems to be the adversarial training scheme.

* The experimental comparisons are problematic. **First**, experiments are conducted only on two small CIFAR datasets, which is far from extensive as claimed in the introduction. Results on other common benchmarks like Tiny-ImageNet or CINIC-10 are required. I also encourage the authors to provide results on large-scaled realistic datasets in [2]. **Second**, the experimental comparisons with other baselines are messy and unfair. FLBoost uses the state-of-the-art method SCAFFOLD as the default client-level method, while FedGen and FedDF [3] use the old method FedAvg. However, the authors did not remind the readers, and directly compared them in Table1, which is quite misleading. I think Table 1 and Table 3 should be changed to include results of the complete combinations between server-level methods (the # is 3) and client-level methods (the # is 4) on all datasets. Even based on the current results, if the client-level method is SCAFFOLD for all three methods in Table 3, I find the accuracy gaps between FLBoost and the other two server-level methods are significantly decreased. **Third**, I think using figures rather than tables to show the convergence is more straightforward. Figure 6 can be put in the appendix to give space for more results.

* The proposed method explicitly violated the privacy protection regulation in FL: 1. Uploading classes statistics on the clients. 2. Recovering images of clients on the server. It is not a good clarification using the violation of other works to defend the proposed method.

## Comments
* Missing related works: client-level method MOON at CVPR'21 [4].
* Symbols not clarified or formulations missing: Symbols inTable 4 are not consistent with those in Section 3.1. The diversity loss is missing both in this submission and FedGen. 

## References
[1] Data-Free Knowledge Distillation for Heterogeneous Federated Learning, ICML'21

[2] Federated Visual Classification with Real-World Data Distribution, ECCV'20

[3] Ensemble Distillation for Robust Model Fusion in Federated Learning, NeurIPS'20

[4] Model-Contrastive Federated Learning, CVPR'21
content.summary_of_the_review: In conclusion, I think this submission has weaknesses in the method novelty, experimental validation, and privacy concern. Thus, I decided to give a rating of 5 at the current stage.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 2
content.comment:
Thank you for your effort put into this paper and the constructive comments to this work. The questions and suggestions about experiments and privacy issues are especially valuable for us. The following are detailed response to each comment.


* The contribution of this paper lies on FocusedKD, EnsembleAtt and AdvLearing, which are introduced to adapt the data imbalance in clients and alleviate the performance drop during model aggregation. In the future we will put more effort to extend this work.


* **First**, in experiment we follow the settings of FedDyn, where the evaluation datasets are CIFAR10 and CIFAR100. These two small datasets may be unconvincing to validate the efficacy of the proposed method. In the revision, we add experiment results on other three datasets in the Appendix A.10, which are MIO-TCD[1], CompCar[2] and Tiny-ImageNet[3] datasets. The first two datasets are large-scale realistic datasets of vehicle classification task. On all these three datasets FLBoost consistently yields higher performance than other methods. Please see the appendix for detailed experiment settings and results. **Second**, FedGen is a client-level method actually, and we forcibly combined them for a fair comparison. As we can see, it gains marginal performance increase compared with SCAFFOLD (0.06% and 0.08% for CIFAR10 and CIFAR100). For FedDF, when using SCAFFOLD as the local optimizer, FLBoost exceeds it by 0.6% and 0.8% for CIFAR10 and CIFAR100. When using FedAvg as the local optimizer, FLBoost exceeds it by 0.9% and 1.3%. We think FLBoost has certain effect. A complete combination between server-level methods and client-level methods is important for deep understanding of the orthogonality of different methods. Due to time limit, we may be unable to conduct this experiment during rebuttal. In the future we will put more effort into it. **Third**, for more precise comparison, we display convergence in form of table following FedDyn. In the revision, we add the figure corresponding to Table 2 in Appendix A.9. In this figure, FLBoost exceeds the other methods in about 150 and 100 rounds for CIFAR10 and CIFAR100, and it achieves distinct performance gain after 1000 rounds. Please see Appendix A.9 for detailed results.


* In the revision, we analyze the privacy issue about FLBoost in Appendix A.8. 
> **Uploading classes statistics on the clients.**
Uploading classes statistics of clients to server may leak private information. One optional solution is using partial local data during local training, as the global model training in FLBoost is based on the *statistics of data involved in current round*. Using this strategy, the clients need to send the statistics of involved data in each round, rather than upload the statistics of total data once before training. If the client designs the data selection properly, the server and data stealer will not know the precise data statistics. Note that partial local training is adopted and tolerated in many methods, such as SCAFFOLD, FedProx and FedFR[4]. Besides, it is common in real-world FL tasks due to the system heterogeneity of clients.
>
> **Recovering images of clients on the server.** Since FLBoost trains a generator to recover the training data of clients, it may violate the privacy protection regulation in FL. However, according to our observation, the generator can only capture the high-level feature pattern of training, which can not be understood by human beings (see Figure 1). Besides, as the generator is trained by all local models, the generated data tend to show shared features of data, which means the attribute of individual data will not be revealed. In addition, according to [5] and [6], the local model itself can be utilized to recover the training data, without using an auxiliary generator. 

[1] Luo Z, Branchaud-Charron F, Lemaire C, et al. MIO-TCD: A new benchmark dataset for vehicle classification and localization[J]. IEEE Transactions on Image Processing, 2018, 27(10): 5129-5141.

[2] Yang L, Luo P, Change Loy C, et al. A large-scale car dataset for fine-grained categorization and verification[C]//Proceedings of the IEEE conference on computer vision and pattern recognition. 2015: 3973-3981.

[3] https://www.kaggle.com/c/tiny-imagenet

[4] Zhuang W, Gan X, Wen Y, et al. Towards Unsupervised Domain Adaptation for Deep Face Recognition under Privacy Constraints via Federated Learning[J]. arXiv preprint arXiv:2105.07606, 2021.

[5] Yin H, Molchanov P, Alvarez J M, et al. Dreaming to distill: Data-free knowledge transfer via deepinversion[C]//Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2020: 8715-8724.

[6] Yin H, Mallya A, Vahdat A, et al. See through Gradients: Image Batch Recovery via GradInversion[C]//Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2021: 16337-16346.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors tackle the data heterogeneity in federated learning and proposed a novel data-free distillation method, namely FLBoost, which consists of a set of algorithms, such as focused knowledge distillation, attention-based ensemble, and adversarial learning schemes to train the global model and the generator.
content.main_review:
This paper is well-written and easy to understand. The motivation is clear and the concept illustration is helpful to capture high-level ideas. The proposed method seems intuitive and technically sound. 

I have a few questions while reading this paper:


- Additional server-side training costs per round: as the proposed method requires additional server-side training, many readers might want to know how long it will take in one communication round. 


- The trade-off between Performance vs Finetuning steps ($I$, $I_g$, and $I_d$): Can you provide an analysis of the effect of the different numbers of $I$, $I_g$, and $I_d$?


- Learning curves for Table 2: can you provide learning curves corresponding to Table 2? It is way more insightful to see plots rather than analyze tables.


- More datasets: please use more datasets and show if the results are consistent since some performances seem marginal compared to the baseline models.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I enjoyed reading the paper. I'll raise my score if my concerns are successfully addressed.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 1
content.comment:
Thank you for your effort put into this paper and the constructive comments to this work. The questions and suggestions about method evaluation are especially valuable for us. The following are detailed response to each comment.


* The training time is related to the hyperparameters $I$, $I_g$, $I_d$ and the active client number $\left \lceil C\cdot K \right \rceil$ in each round. In our experiment settings, the training time in one communication round for FedAVG, FedProx, FedDyn, SCAFFOLD, FedGen, FedDF and FLBoost are 78, 82, 83, 93, 165, 188, 194 seconds respectively. The last three DFKD based methods require roughly double time of the first four methods. The experiments are conducted on a machine with Intel(R) Xeon(R) CPU E5-2690 0 $@$ 2.90GHz, 32GB main memory and GPU GTX TITAN.


* According to our experience, too low and too high $I$ will influence the performance. When $I$ is too low, the global model and generator can not be trained sufficiently. In our experiments, $I=5$ will gain marginal performance increase compared with SCAFFOLD. When $I$ is too high, the performance will suffer a decrease. Note that the pseudo data can only capture the high-level feature distribution of real data. They are used to alleviate the performance drop during model aggregation. Higher $I$ will make the global model fit the pseudo data and forget the real data information. $I_g$ should be smaller than $I_d$, because the generator is easy to generate hard samples that maximize $L_{md}$, while the global model needs more effort to minimize $L_{md}$.


* We add the figure of learning curves corresponding to Table 2 in Appendix A.9. In this figure, FLBoost exceeds the other methods in about 150 and 100 rounds for CIFAR10 and CIFAR100, and it achieves distinct performance gain after 1000 rounds. Please see Appendix A.9 for detailed results.


* We add experiment results on more datasets in Appendix A.10. Due to time limit, we only test three datasets: MIO-TCD[1], CompCar[2], and Tiny-ImageNet[3]. The first two datasets are large-scale realistic datasets of vehicle classification task. On all these three datasets FLBoost consistently yields higher performance than other methods. Please see the appendix for detailed experiment settings and results.

[1] Luo Z, Branchaud-Charron F, Lemaire C, et al. MIO-TCD: A new benchmark dataset for vehicle classification and localization[J]. IEEE Transactions on Image Processing, 2018, 27(10): 5129-5141.

[2] Yang L, Luo P, Change Loy C, et al. A large-scale car dataset for fine-grained categorization and verification[C]//Proceedings of the IEEE conference on computer vision and pattern recognition. 2015: 3973-3981.

[3] https://www.kaggle.com/c/tiny-imagenet
